limitations: NOT WIRED INTO ANY PRODUCTION WRITE PATH. resolve.ts:151 and prepare.ts:328 still update `authored` without appending a revision — both files are outside this agent's ownership, so the wiring is filed as changeRequests. Today the chain only grows when a caller invokes commitAuthoredState / appendAuthoredRevision explicitly (the smoke suite does).
Not exported from src/release/index.ts (barrel not owned) — callers must deep-import src/release/revisions.js until the changeRequest lands.

Full-snapshot storage: every revision embeds the entire authored state. Fine at today's sizes (tens of slot values); a site with thousands of authored slots and a long edit history will want a diff or content-addressed store, which this deliberately is NOT.

The hash covers the whole captured snapshot INCLUDING `updatedAt`. Content edits move updatedAt in lock step (instance.ts foldResolutionIntoAuthored only touches it when something changed), so this holds in practice — but a caller that bumps updatedAt alone would produce a new hash with an empty `change`.
No concurrency control beyond the `wx` write: two processes appending at the same instant produce one success and one EEXIST throw. There is no lock, retry, or queue.
No pruning/retention policy and no CLI surface (no `release:revisions` command); the chain grows without bound and is only reachable from code.
loadRevisionChain reads and parses every record to return the chain; a head-only read still costs O(chain).

The r999/r1000 boundary test seeds r000..r998 by writing records directly rather than through appendAuthoredRevision (quadratic otherwise). The crossing appends themselves use the public API, but the 999 seeded records are not proof that 999 real appends would succeed — only that a 1,001-long chain on disk loads and extends correctly.

The boundary is tested only at r999/r1000. The same widening happens again at r9999/r10000; the numeric sort handles it by construction (Number.parseInt has no digit ceiling here) but no test crosses that second boundary.

loadRevisionChain now reads and parses 1,001 records to answer headRevision at that chain length — the pre-existing O(chain) head read (already listed above) becomes a real cost exactly where this fix makes long chains possible.

sortFix.defect: loadRevisionChain sorted revision directory names LEXICOGRAPHICALLY (a bare `.sort()`), then required `revision.revisionId === revisionIdForIndex(index)`. Because `revisionIdForIndex` deliberately WIDENS past r999 rather than wrapping, the moment r1000 exists the lexical order is "... r099, r100, r1000, r101 ..." and position 101 holds r1000 where r101 is expected. loadRevisionChain threw, and with it headRevision, appendAuthoredRevision, getRevision and restoreAuthoredRevision — the project's chain became permanently unloadable at exactly the point a Visual Editor undo history reaches 1,000 revisions.
sortFix.fix: Order NUMERICALLY. A new exported inverse, `revisionIndexForId` (src/release/revisions.ts:178-180), parses the index out of the id; loadRevisionChain sorts by that index (src/release/revisions.ts:196-203), with a name tie-break so a hand-written id that no `revisionIdForIndex` can emit (`r0001` beside `r001`) still fails the existing id check deterministically rather than nondeterministically.
sortFix.notCappedNotWrapped: The widening contract is untouched: `revisionIdForIndex` is byte-identical, no chain length cap was introduced, and no id wraps. Only the READ ordering changed.
sortFix.existingIdsUnchanged: No on-disk revision id changes. The fix reorders names after readdir and writes nothing; the two real release projects used as fixtures were byte-checked untouched by 27A.22/27A.23 in the same run.
